🖥 Some bombs were ‘exclusively built for use against Iran’: Acting defense minister

📌 Tehran, IRNA- Iran’s acting defense minister says the country has faced a hybrid war of unprecedented scale, involving cyber, military, proxy and counter-revolutionary elements, with some bombs specifically manufactured for use against Iran.

Majid Ibn al-Reza, caretaker of the Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics, made the remarks in separate meetings with parliamentary commissions on agriculture, environment, and planning and budget, where he presented a report on the latest imposed war and the performance of the country’s defense industry.
​
“The enemy entered the field with a combined pattern, using cyber tools, military forces, proxy forces and counter-revolutionary elements, employing all its capabilities,” Ibn al-Reza said.
​
He added that “some weapons were used for the first time, and even some bombs were specifically manufactured for use against Iran.”
​
The acting defense minister described the recent war as “one of the most unprecedented in history from various aspects,” calling it “the first large-scale missile war, the first large-scale drone war,” with the highest volume of air operations and among the first wars in terms of extensive use of various defense technologies.
​
Despite the intense fighting, Ibn al-Reza said the defense industry continued its activities without interruption, even under the most difficult wartime conditions.
​
“Production of defense products did not stop; in some areas, we saw a two- to several-fold growth,” he said.
​
He also noted that capabilities were upgraded during the war, adding that “in different waves of attacks, we operated differently and more effectively than before in terms of technology and performance.”
​
The acting defense minister said Iran is preparing for “threats of the next 50 years,” with the ministry relying on capable managers, motivated staff and expert elites to conduct future studies and design the path forward.
​
“Our movement will be toward maximum use of national capacity,” he said.

🇮🇶🇪🇬 Hamas Moves Between Baghdad and Washington

A Hamas delegation led by Osama Hamdan was reported to have met in Baghdad with Hadi al-Ameri, head of Iraq’s Badr Organization and a central figure in the country’s Iran-aligned political and militia network.

If confirmed, the meeting would underline a familiar fact: Hamas still operates through the regional relationships built with Iran and its partners. Baghdad is not Doha or Ankara. But it is part of the same political geography in which Hamas’s external leadership has sought money, protection, influence, and military support.

At the same time, Washington is dealing with Hamas through a very different channel.

On Sunday, Jared Kushner, President Trump’s envoy, met Khalil al-Hayya, Hamas’s overall leader, in El Alamein, Egypt. It was Kushner’s second meeting with al-Hayya after their October 2025 talks helped produce the ceasefire and hostage-release agreement. The meeting marked another break with Washington’s long-standing policy of refusing direct engagement with Hamas, which the United States designates as a terrorist organization. 

Kushner was joined by Nickolay Mladenov and Tony Blair, senior envoys of the U.S.-backed Board of Peace. 

The body is intended to oversee the Gaza roadmap, including a planned transfer of Gaza’s civilian administration to a Palestinian technocratic committee and a process for placing Hamas weapons under that committee’s control. Egypt, Qatar, and Turkey also sent senior diplomats. 

The central dispute was not diplomatic etiquette. It was sequencing.

Hamas told Kushner it would begin handing over weapons only after Israel publicly committed to the plan’s terms. Israel has maintained that it will not withdraw until Hamas is fully disarmed. 

The American-backed framework asks each side to move first while promising that the other side eventually will. 

Freddy Eytan, a former senior Israeli Foreign Ministry official and researcher at the Jerusalem Center for Foreign Affairs, criticized the meeting as a step toward legitimizing Hamas. In an opinion piece, he wrote: “How can Donald Trump authorize direct negotiations with a terrorist organization?” 

He argued that Israel should “be uncompromising on security issues and obtain robust guarantees from the United States.” This is Eytan’s assessment, not an account from the negotiating room. 

Hamas can speak with an Iran-aligned militia leader in Baghdad while its leadership negotiates with a U.S. envoy in Egypt. 

The organization is not being asked to choose between those channels. It is being asked to surrender weapons while keeping both open.
